newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Metaleurop sees strong zinc/lead outlook.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Metaleurop sees strong zinc/lead outlook.

text.p: Lead and zinc producer Metaleurop sees a positive outlook for its two most important products, after mixed fortunes during much of 1996.
"In my view, zinc will be one of the stars over the next two years," group chairman Helmut Stodieck told Reuters in an interview.
"I think for zinc $1,300 a tonne is certainly achievable. But it is a question of when (the rally) starts," he added.
"A price of $1,300 to $1,400 would have a strong effect on our results and could be called normal."
In 1996 lead prices have been well above their long term averages while zinc prices have remained firmly below theirs.
For lead, he said, fundamentals pointed to a positive price outlook, although recent high levels might not be maintained.
"I personally see a strong lead market for this winter/spring season and there may be a softening of the price for the rest of the year."
Metaleurop is the Western world's second largest lead producer with annual output of 360,000 tonnes. It is the seventh largest producer of zinc with output of 245,000 tonnes.
"I was not really surprised at zinc's weakness in 1996," Stodieck said. "Stocks are still putting pressure on the market and everyone knows that zinc is available."
LME zinc stocks fell sharply in 1995 and 1996 to 550,000 tonnes from a peak late in 1994 of over 1.2 million tonnes.
"In my view the stock decrease will go on for some time and I'm sure this will have an impact on the market price.
"In the region of 450,000 to 500,000 tonnes we should feel a price effect from this development."
Stodieck said he still supported the idea of voluntary production cuts among Western smelters, who were partly to blame for the glut of metal in the early 1990s.
In February Stodieck had said Western European refined zinc capacity should be cut by 100,000 tonnes to reduce oversupply.
But Metaleurop officials suggested such cuts were unlikely.
"Closing down a plant is terribly difficult for economic and social reasons," Metaleurop board member Christian Bue said.
In the long term the main growth area for zinc consumption would be galvanising, which accounted for about half world 1995 zinc consumption of 7.4 million tonnes, Stodieck said.
He said zinc demand would increase at similar rates to those during the last decade. Between 1985 and 1995 total zinc demand rose 32 percent but galvanising offtake shot up by 51 percent.
For lead, long-term growth in demand depended on the battery industry. In 1995 some 70 percent of the 5.4 million tonne market was used in batteries, according to Metaleurop.
"Under "normal' conditions, without an electric car, I would see (demand) developing more or less in the same way (as during the last decade)," Stodieck said.
Between 1985 and 1995 Metaleurop estimated lead demand grew 22 percent overall and by 47 percent in the batteries sector.
In 1997 Metaleurop and other lead producers were likely to be able to maintain the high physical premiums of around $90 a tonne they commanded in 1996, Christian Bue said.
"Lead is now stable and the price should remain more or less stable as well as treatment charges and premiums," he said.
Metaleurop would continue to focus on the European market where its core customers were, and aimed to boost the amount of secondary lead and zinc it produced.
Stodieck said Metaleurop was heading for a positive net profit figure in 1995/96, improving further in 1996/97 to between 60 million and 200 million francs.
The company posted losses between 1992/93 and 1994/95. But sales of non-core business and big cuts in personnel in recent years have contributed to its expected return to the black.
Stodieck said the company would be looking to raise fresh capital soon, but he would not specify when.
